claims.text: Limiting differential atomic mobility during nucleation promotes homogeneous, single-phase noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Confining equimolar noble-metal precursors within a tailored inert host matrix limits differential atomic mobility.
Confinement ensures near-simultaneous reduction and nucleation of the constituent elements.
Without confinement, intrinsic differences in reduction kinetics cause sequential reduction.
Sequential reduction can result in phase segregation and uncontrolled particle morphology.
The proposed starting material is an equimolar mixture of noble-metal precursors, exemplified by Pt, Ir, Au, Pd, and Rh.
The controlled comparison uses identical synthesis routes differing only in whether the precursors are placed in a mobility-restricting confinement matrix.
The synthesis rapidly heats the precursor system to approximately 923 K and then immediately quenches it under an inert atmosphere.
Rapid processing at 923 K can produce uniform alloys, whereas slower heating can produce phase-separated particles.
Confinement forms and stabilizes ultra-small nuclei that serve as uniform seeding sites.
Restricting atomic motion minimizes intrinsic differences in both reduction kinetics and diffusivities.
With more atom types and limited free-atom mobility, stochastic formation of a random alloy becomes more likely.
Differences in elemental reduction and diffusion can cause some metals to nucleate earlier, producing phase separation and elemental segregation.
The confined route will yield homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The confined route will yield smaller particles with a narrower size distribution than the unconfined route.
The confined route will preserve high surface-atom exposure.
The hypothesis applies to equimolar noble-metal systems containing five or more elements under rapid thermal processing near 923 K.
The hypothesis may not apply to non-noble-metal systems with very different reduction properties or when the matrix changes heat transfer or chemistry.
Matrix-induced changes in heat transfer or surface interactions could confound attribution of the outcome to restricted mobility.
The hypothesis is falsified if confined and unconfined syntheses show similar phase segregation, elemental segregation, and morphology under identical thermal conditions.
